p.src: As Xifeng was comforting Ping'er, all the young ladies suddenly came in. She hastened to offer them seats, and Ping'er poured tea for them. Xifeng laughed. “What a full gathering today! Anyone would think I had sent out invitations.” Tanchun replied with a smile, “We have come about two matters—one concerns me, the other Fourth Sister—and we also bring a message from Grandmother.” “What can be so important?” Xifeng asked with a laugh. Tanchun said, smiling, “We have founded a poetry club, but at its very first meeting not everyone was present. The others were too softhearted to enforce the rules, so everything fell into disorder. I think we must have you serve as our censor, perfectly stern and impartial. Then Fourth Sister needs all sorts of materials to paint the garden, and many are missing. We reported it to Grandmother, and she said, ‘There may still be some left from years ago beneath the rear storied building. Have a search made. If there are any, bring them out; if not, send someone to buy them.’” Xifeng laughed. “I cannot compose anything, wet or dry. Surely you do not only want me there to eat?” “You need not compose anything merely because you do not know how,” said Tanchun. “You need only keep watch for anyone among us who shirks her duties or grows lazy, and impose whatever penalty she deserves.” Xifeng laughed. “Do not try to fool me. I have guessed your scheme. You are not really inviting me to be the club censor! Plainly you want me to be your moneyed patron. Whatever sort of club you have formed, its members must surely take turns as hostess. Your monthly allowances are not enough, so you devised this trick to drag me in and ask me for money. Is that not the true idea?” Her speech set everyone laughing. Li Wan laughed. “You truly have a crystal heart and a glass body—nothing escapes you.” Xifeng laughed. “And you call yourself their eldest sister-in-law! The young ladies were entrusted to you so that you might teach them reading, proper conduct, and needlework. When they go astray, you ought to advise them. Now that they have founded a poetry club, which can cost only a little, are you simply going to ignore them? Grandmother and Madam are another matter; they are venerable ladies of rank. But your monthly allowance is ten taels of silver, twice as much as ours. And because Grandmother and Madam say that you are a poor widow without a livelihood, whose allowance cannot suffice and who also has a boy to support, they add another ten taels to make your income equal to theirs. You have also been allotted land in the garden, from which you collect rent. When the annual allotments are distributed at year's end, you receive one of the very best shares. Including mistress and servants, your whole household numbers fewer than ten, while all your food and clothing still come from the common purse. Added together, your income must amount to four or five hundred taels a year. If you took out one or two hundred taels each year to let them enjoy themselves, how many years would you have to do it? Once they have each married, surely you will not still be expected to pay for them?”

p.src: Li Wan laughed. “Listen to her! I said one sentence, and she went wild, pouring out cartloads of vulgar, shameless marketplace talk—the sort of petty reckoning and haggling over every fraction that only a coarse country bumpkin could relish. It is a wonder that this creature, born as a young lady into a distinguished family of great officials and scholars, and married into another such house, should still behave this way. Had she been born a boy in some poor humble family, who knows how base, glib, and venomous she might have become! You would scheme every person under heaven out of all they possess! You even struck Ping'er yesterday. How could you bring yourself to raise your hand against her? Did all that vile liquor go pouring into a dog's belly instead of your own? I was so angry that I meant to come and take up Ping'er's grievance. I considered it for half the day, but since it was the rare auspicious day when ‘a dog's tail grows a pointed tip,’ I feared Grandmother might be distressed, and so I did not come. Yet my anger has never truly subsided. And today you have provoked me all over again. It would not be enough for you to pick up Ping'er's shoes for her—you two ought simply to exchange places.” Everyone laughed at this. Xifeng hurriedly said with a laugh, “So you did not really come to see me about poetry or painting. All this severity is to avenge Ping'er! I never imagined Ping'er had such a stalwart champion in you. Had I known, even if a ghost had seized my hand and forced me to strike her, I would not have done it. Come here, Miss Ping! Before Eldest Mistress and all the young ladies, I shall apologize to you. Please forgive my disgraceful behavior when I was drunk.” At this, everyone burst out laughing again. Li Wan asked Ping'er with a smile, “Well? Did I not say that I would make certain justice was done for you?” Ping'er smiled. “Even so, I cannot bear being made the subject of all you ladies' jokes.” “What do you mean, you cannot bear it?” said Li Wan. “You have me on your side. Quickly fetch the keys and tell your mistress to open the storeroom, so that we may search for the materials.”

p.src: Xifeng laughed. “Dear sister-in-law, go back to the Garden with them for now. I was just about to settle the rice accounts when the First Lady sent for me again. I do not know what she wants, but I must go and see her. And the extra clothes you will need for the New Year have not yet been put in hand.” Li Wan laughed. “I want nothing to do with all that. Just finish my business so that I can go and rest, and these young ladies will stop plaguing me.” Xifeng hastily replied with a laugh, “Dear sister-in-law, spare me a little time. You have always cared for me most. Why have you stopped caring for me today, all for Ping’er’s sake? You used to urge me to take care of myself, saying that however much business I had, I ought to find a moment to rest. Yet today you are hounding me to death. Besides, it would not matter if other people’s New Year clothes were delayed, but if the young ladies’ clothes are late, the responsibility will be yours. Wouldn’t the Old Lady blame you for meddling in other people’s affairs when you could have settled matters with a single ready word? I would rather bear the blame myself than dare to implicate you.” Li Wan laughed. “Listen to her! Isn’t that beautifully put? What a clever tongue she has! Let me ask you plainly: are you going to take charge of this poetry club or not?” Xifeng laughed. “What a question! If I do not join the club and contribute a little money, I shall become a rebel against Prospect Garden. How could I still expect to be fed here? I shall assume office first thing tomorrow morning, dismount, pay homage to my seal, and begin by putting down fifty taels of silver for you to use gradually in entertaining the club. After a few days, since I can compose neither poetry nor prose and am nothing but a vulgar creature, whether I ‘supervise’ you or not, once you have the money, you will surely drive me out!” At this, everyone burst out laughing again. Xifeng said, “In a little while I shall open the storeroom upstairs and have everything of that kind brought out for you to inspect. Keep and use whatever is suitable; if anything is lacking, give me a list and I shall have it bought for you. I shall cut the painting silk for you. The design is not with the Lady, however; Master Zhen still has it over there. I am warning you so that you do not go there only to be rebuffed. I shall send someone to fetch it, then have both it and the silk delivered to the craftsmen to be treated with alum. How would that be?” Li Wan nodded and laughed. “That is very good of you. If you truly do all that, then we shall be satisfied. Since that is settled, let us go home. If she fails to send the things, we shall come back and pester her again.” With that, she led the young ladies away. Xifeng said, “No one else could have stirred up all this business. It was entirely Baoyu’s doing.” Hearing this, Li Wan hurriedly turned back and laughed. “Why, we came precisely on Baoyu’s account, yet we forgot all about him. He missed the first meeting of the club.

p.src: Just as they were about to leave, they saw a young maid helping Nanny Lai into the room. Xifeng and the others hurriedly rose and said with smiles, “Please sit down, Nanny.” They all congratulated her as well. Nanny Lai sat on the edge of the kang and laughed. “It is a joyful occasion for me and for the masters too. Without our masters’ favor, how could such happiness ever have come to us? Yesterday, madam also sent Cai to bestow gifts on us, and my grandson kowtowed toward the residence from the gate.” Li Wan asked with a smile, “When will he take up his post?” Nanny Lai sighed. “I have no say over them. Let them do as they please! The other day, when he kowtowed to me at home, I gave him a good scolding. I said, ‘Listen, my boy! Do not think that because you are now an official you may swagger about and tyrannize over people! You are thirty years old this year. Though born into a bondservant family, from the moment you left your mother’s womb our masters graciously allowed you to live apart from household service. Thanks above to the masters’ great blessing and below to your parents’ care, you studied and learned your characters like a young gentleman, while maids, a wife, and nurses waited on you as though you were a phoenix, raising you to manhood. How could you know even how the two words “bondservant” are written? You know only how to enjoy yourself. You know nothing of the hardships endured by your grandfather and your father, who struggled for two or three generations before finally managing to raise a creature like you. From childhood you suffered one illness and mishap after another, and we spent enough silver on you to have cast a man of solid silver. When you reached twenty, our masters again favored you by permitting you to purchase an official rank. Just look how many men of respectable birth are starving and going hungry! You, the offspring of bondservants, had better take care not to exhaust your good fortune! After ten years of ease, you somehow contrived to petition the masters, and now you have been selected for an appointment. A prefectural or county official may hold a low rank, but his responsibilities are great. The magistrate of a prefecture is the father and mother of all the people in his district. If you fail to behave properly, serve the state loyally, and honor your masters, I fear that Heaven itself will not tolerate you.’” Li Wan and Xifeng both laughed. “You worry too much. From what we have seen, he seems quite a good man. In the earlier years he came in to see us twice, but he has not visited for several years now. At New Year and on birthdays, we see nothing but his name on the gift lists. The other day, when he came to kowtow to the Old Lady and the Lady, we saw him in the Old Lady’s courtyard dressed in his new official robes. They made him look quite imposing, and he has grown stouter than before. Now that he has obtained office, you ought to be rejoicing. Why fret over all these things instead? If he should misbehave, his father is still there to deal with him. You need only enjoy your own comfort. Whenever you have leisure, come here in a sedan chair, play cards with the Old Lady all day, and spend the day chatting. Who would have the heart to treat you badly?

p.src: Ping'er poured some tea. Nanny Lai hurriedly rose to accept it and said with a smile, “You could simply have told one of the young maids to pour it, miss. You honor me too greatly again.” As she drank her tea, she continued, “You don't know, madam. All these youngsters must be kept under strict discipline. Even with such strictness, they still seize any chance to cause trouble and make their elders worry. Those who understand say the youngsters are merely mischievous; those who do not accuse them of using the family's wealth and power to bully others, thereby damaging their masters' good name as well. When they exasperate me beyond endurance, I often summon their fathers and give them a scolding; only then do matters improve a little.” Then, pointing at Baoyu, she said, “Do not take offense at me. The Master barely disciplines you at all, and the Old Lady always steps in to protect you. When the Master was young, who among us did not see your grandfather beat him? When he was young, the Master was never as utterly fearless as you are. Then there was the First Master. Though mischievous, he never gathered a whole pack around him as you do, yet he too was beaten every day. And over in the eastern mansion, your cousin Zhen's grandfather had a temper that only added fuel to the flames. Once he said he was angry, he treated his own son as though he were interrogating a thief! From what I now see with my own eyes and hear with my own ears, Master Zhen disciplines his son much as the old forebear did in those days, only he does it without rhyme or reason. Since he never governs his own conduct, how can he blame his younger kinsmen and nephews for not fearing him? If you have sense, you will be glad to hear me say this. If you do not, you may be too polite to answer me aloud, but goodness knows how you are cursing me in your heart.” While she was speaking, Steward Lai's wife arrived, followed by Zhou Rui's wife and Zhang Cai's wife, who had all come to report on household matters. Xifeng laughed. “Here comes the daughter-in-law to fetch her mother-in-law.” Steward Lai's wife smiled. “I have not come to fetch the old lady, but to ask whether you ladies and young misses will honor us with your presence.” Hearing this, Nanny Lai laughed. “How muddleheaded I am! Instead of discussing the business that brought me, I have been rambling on about stale old tales. Our boy has been selected for office, and since all our relatives and friends wish to congratulate him, we can hardly avoid holding a banquet at home. At first I thought of holding it for one day, but then it seemed wrong to invite this person and not that one. Then I reflected that it is through our masters' great blessing that we have received such undreamed-of honor, and I would willingly spend my whole fortune on it.

p.src: “So I told his father to hold three successive days of feasting. On the first day, we shall set several tables and arrange a theatrical performance in our shabby little garden, inviting the Old Lady, the senior ladies, the young ladies and the young misses to enjoy a day's diversion. In the outer reception hall there will be another performance and several more tables, so that the masters and young gentlemen may honor us with their presence. On the second day we shall entertain relatives and friends, and on the third we shall invite our companions from both mansions. Three lively days will display both the great favor our masters have shown us and the honor it has brought our family.” Li Wan and Xifeng both laughed. “What day have you chosen? We shall certainly go, and perhaps the Old Lady will be in the mood to go as well.” Steward Lai's wife hastened to reply, “We have chosen the fourteenth. Everything depends on whether our old lady still has enough standing with you.” Xifeng laughed. “I cannot speak for anyone else, but I shall certainly go. But let me warn you now: I shall bring no congratulatory gift and give no gratuities. I shall eat my fill and leave, so you must not laugh at me.” Steward Lai's wife laughed. “How can you say such a thing, madam? If you wish to reward us, a mere twenty or thirty thousand taels of silver will suffice.” Nanny Lai laughed. “I have just invited the Old Lady, and she too said she would come. It seems my old face still carries some weight.” After giving them several more reminders, she rose to leave. Then, noticing Zhou Rui's wife, she remembered something and said, “There is one more question I must ask you, madam. What offense did Mistress Zhou's son commit that made you dismiss him from service?” Hearing this, Xifeng smiled. “Indeed, I meant to tell your daughter-in-law, but with so much business I forgot. Mistress Lai, when you return, tell your husband that neither mansion is to employ that fellow. Let him go his own way.”

We shall certainly go, and perhaps the Old Lady will be in the mood to go as well.”
Steward Lai's wife hastened to reply, “We have chosen the fourteenth. Everything depends on whether our old lady still has enough standing with you.”
Xifeng laughed. “I cannot speak for anyone else, but I shall certainly go.
But let me warn you now: I shall bring no congratulatory gift and give no gratuities. I shall eat my fill and leave, so you must not laugh at me.”
Steward Lai's wife laughed. “How can you say such a thing, madam?
If you wish to reward us, a mere twenty or thirty thousand taels of silver will suffice.”
Nanny Lai laughed. “I have just invited the Old Lady, and she too said she would come. It seems my old face still carries some weight.”

After giving them several more reminders, she rose to leave. Then, noticing Zhou Rui's wife, she remembered something and said, “There is one more question I must ask you, madam. What offense did Mistress Zhou's son commit that made you dismiss him from service?”
Hearing this, Xifeng smiled. “Indeed, I meant to tell your daughter-in-law, but with so much business I forgot.
Mistress Lai, when you return, tell your husband that neither mansion is to employ that fellow. Let him go his own way.”

p.src: Steward Lai's wife had no choice but to assent. Zhou Rui's wife hurriedly knelt and pleaded for mercy. Nanny Lai quickly asked, “What happened? Tell me, and let me judge the matter.” Xifeng said, “The other day, on my birthday, before the drinking had even begun inside, her son was already drunk. When gifts arrived from my mother's family, instead of making arrangements outside, he sat there abusing people and did not even send the gifts in. Only after two women came in did he lead the young servants in to carry them. The young servants did well enough, but he lost his grip on one box he was carrying and scattered steamed buns all over the courtyard. After the visitors had gone, I sent Caiming to reprimand him, but he gave Caiming a thorough scolding instead. What else could I do but dismiss such a lawless little bastard!” Nanny Lai laughed. “I wondered what grave affair it was, but it is only this. Listen to me, madam. If he has done wrong, beat him and scold him until he reforms, but you absolutely must not drive him away. He is not like one of our hereditary household servants; he belongs to the retinue that accompanied the Lady here at her marriage. If you simply dismiss him, madam, the Lady will lose face. In my opinion, you should have him given a few strokes as a warning against future misconduct, and then keep him in service as before. Even if you show no consideration for his mother, you should consider the Lady.” After hearing her out, Xifeng said to Steward Lai's wife, “Very well, then. Give him forty strokes and forbid him to drink from now on.” Steward Lai's wife agreed. Zhou Rui's wife kowtowed and rose, then tried to kowtow to Nanny Lai as well, but Steward Lai's wife held her back, and she desisted. The three women then departed, while Li Wan and the others returned to the garden. That evening, as promised, Xifeng had a great quantity of old painting materials taken from storage and delivered to the garden. Baochai and the others spent some time sorting through them, but only half the various articles were usable. They made a list of the remaining half and sent it to Xifeng so that replacements could be purchased; there is no need to relate the details.

p.src: One day, the silk prepared outside was brought in together with the preliminary sketches. Baoyu went to Xichun's quarters every day to help her. Tanchun, Li Wan, Yingchun, Baochai, and the others also often went there to sit at leisure, partly to watch the painting and partly because it gave them a chance to meet. Finding the weather cool and the nights gradually lengthening, Baochai went to her mother's rooms to discuss preparing some needlework. During the day she paid her respects twice at Grandmother Jia's and Lady Wang's apartments, where she naturally had to sit agreeably and chat for a while; she also had to spend some time talking with the girls in the garden. Thus she had little leisure by day, and every night she worked at her needlework by lamplight until the third watch before retiring. Every year after the spring and autumn equinoxes, Daiyu was certain to suffer a coughing illness. That autumn, Grandmother Jia had been in high spirits and Daiyu had joined the outings several times, which had inevitably overtired her. Recently her cough had returned and seemed worse than usual, so she no longer went out but remained in her own rooms recuperating. At times, when boredom weighed on her, she longed for one of the girls to come and chat with her as a diversion; yet when Baochai and the others came to visit, after barely three or five sentences she would grow weary of them again. Everyone made allowances for her illness and knew that she had always been physically delicate and could not bear the slightest distress; therefore, even when she received them inattentively or neglected the courtesies, no one reproached her severely.

p.src: That day Baochai came to visit her, and their conversation turned to her illness. Baochai said, “The physicians who attend this household are all fairly good, but their medicines never seem to help you. Why not ask some more accomplished doctor to examine you? Would it not be wonderful if he cured you? Every year it torments you all through spring and summer; you are neither an old woman nor a little child—what sort of state is this? This cannot be allowed to go on.” “It would be no use,” replied Daiyu. “I know that an illness like mine can never be cured. Never mind the times when I am ill; you need only look at the state I am in even on my good days to know that.” Baochai nodded. “That is precisely the point. The ancients said, ‘Those who eat grain live.’ Yet what you usually eat is not enough to nourish your vitality, blood, or spirits, and that is no good thing.” Daiyu sighed. “‘Life and death are ordained by fate; wealth and rank are decreed by Heaven.’ Such things cannot be forced by human effort. This year it actually seems rather worse than in former years.” While speaking, she had already coughed two or three times. Baochai said, “When I looked at your prescription yesterday, I thought it contained far too much ginseng and cinnamon bark. They may restore vitality and strengthen the spirits, but the medicine should not be too heating. In my view, the first priority is to calm the liver and strengthen the stomach. Once the liver fire is subdued, it can no longer overcome the earth element; and when the stomach's vital energy is sound, food and drink will nourish the body. Each morning, take one liang of the finest bird's nest and five qian of rock sugar, and simmer them into a porridge in a small silver pot. If you make a habit of eating it, it will do you more good than medicine; nothing is better for nourishing the yin and replenishing the vital energy.”

p.src: Daiyu sighed. “You have always treated people extremely well, but I am terribly suspicious by nature and used to imagine that you harbored treachery in your heart. The other day, however, you told me that reading frivolous books was harmful and offered me such sound advice that I became deeply grateful to you. I was entirely in the wrong before and have remained mistaken until now. When I think it over carefully, my mother died early, and I have neither sisters nor brothers. I am fifteen this year, yet not one person has ever instructed me as you did the other day. No wonder Yun always says how good you are. Whenever I heard her praise you in the past, it made me uncomfortable; only after experiencing it myself yesterday did I understand. If you had said what I did, I would never have let you off lightly; yet you took no offense and instead gave me such good counsel. Clearly I had only been misleading myself. If I had not come to understand you the other day, I would never have said any of this to you today. As for what you just said about eating bird's-nest porridge, bird's nest itself is easy enough to obtain; but merely because my health is poor and this illness returns every year, there is no reason to make a great fuss over it. Calling doctors, decocting medicines, and procuring ginseng and cinnamon have already turned the whole household upside down. If I now invent some new demand and ask them to make bird's-nest porridge, the Old Lady, Lady Wang, and Cousin Feng may say nothing, but the old serving-women and maids below stairs are bound to think me far too troublesome. Look at the people here: merely because the Old Lady is especially fond of Baoyu and Feng, they eye those two jealously and make all manner of remarks behind their backs. What, then, must they say of me? Besides, I am not a true mistress of this household. I came here as a helpless dependent, and they already find plenty to dislike about me. If I still fail to know my place, why invite them to curse me?” Baochai said, “If you put it that way, I am in the same position as you.” “How can you compare yourself with me?” asked Daiyu. “You have a mother and an elder brother; you have businesses and land here, and your family still owns houses and property back home. You are only staying here without charge because you are relatives; in all matters, great or small, you do not cost this household so much as half a coin, and you can leave whenever you please. I possess nothing at all. My food, clothing, and every daily necessity, down to a blade of grass or a scrap of paper, are provided just as they are for the daughters of this house. How could those petty people fail to resent me all the more?” Baochai laughed. “In the end, the family will have no more to spend than the cost of one additional dowry. There is no need to worry about that yet.” Hearing this, Daiyu involuntarily blushed and said with a smile, “Just when I had begun to regard you as a serious person and confided all my troubles to you, you turn around and make fun of me.” Baochai laughed. “I may be teasing you, but it is nevertheless the truth. Do not worry. As long as I remain here, I shall keep you company and help you pass the time.”

p.src: Whatever grievances or troubles you have, you need only tell me. If there is anything I can do, I shall naturally help you through it. I do have an elder brother, as you know, but apart from having a mother, which leaves me a little better off than you, there is not much difference between us. You and I may be said to share the same affliction. You are a sensible person yourself; why sigh like Sima Niu that you have no brothers? What you said just now is also true: it is better to avoid an extra complication than to invite one. Tomorrow I shall go home and speak to Mother. I expect we still have some there, so I will send you a few taels. Then the maids can prepare it for you every day; it will cost less and cause no great commotion.” Daiyu hurriedly smiled. “The medicine itself is a small matter; what is precious is your great kindness to me.” “It is hardly worth mentioning!” said Baochai. I only fear that I may fail to show due consideration to everyone. I am afraid I may have tired you, so I shall leave for now.” “Come again this evening and talk with me for a while,” said Daiyu. Baochai promised that she would and then departed; there is no more to tell of this.

p.src: Daiyu drank a couple of mouthfuls of thin rice gruel and reclined on her bed again. Unexpectedly, before the sun had set, the weather changed and rain began to patter down. The lingering autumn rain fell through fitful shifts of light and gloom. Dusk gradually deepened into murky darkness, while raindrops beating on the tips of the bamboo made the scene still more desolate. Knowing that Baochai would be unable to come, she casually picked up a book beneath the lamp. It proved to be Miscellaneous Yuefu Verses, containing poems such as “Lament from an Autumn Bower” and “Lament of Parting.” Daiyu could not help being moved, and her feelings found expression in verse. She composed a poem entitled “On Parting,” modeled on the form of “Spring River, Flowers, Moon and Night,” and named it “Autumn Window on a Windy, Rainy Evening.” The poem ran:

The poem ran:

p.src: Autumn flowers fade in sorrow, autumn grasses turn yellow; the autumn lamp burns bright through the long autumn night.

u.src: Autumn flowers fade in sorrow, autumn grasses turn yellow; the autumn lamp burns bright through the long autumn night.

p.src: Already autumn at my window seems endless—how can I bear the wind and rain that deepen the desolation?

u.src: Already autumn at my window seems endless—how can I bear the wind and rain that deepen the desolation?

p.src: How swiftly the wind and rain come to swell autumn’s grief! They startle me awake from green dreams by the autumn window.

u.src: How swiftly the wind and rain come to swell autumn’s grief!
They startle me awake from green dreams by the autumn window.

p.src: Embracing autumn sorrow, I cannot bear to sleep; I move the weeping candle toward the autumn screen.

u.src: Embracing autumn sorrow, I cannot bear to sleep; I move the weeping candle toward the autumn screen.

p.src: The tearful candle flickers on its low stand, stirring grief, illuminating sorrow, and awakening thoughts of parting.

u.src: The tearful candle flickers on its low stand, stirring grief, illuminating sorrow, and awakening thoughts of parting.

p.src: Into whose autumn courtyard does no wind enter? At what autumn window is no rain heard?

u.src: Into whose autumn courtyard does no wind enter?
At what autumn window is no rain heard?

p.src: My silken quilt cannot withstand the autumn wind; the waning water clock urges the autumn rain to greater haste.

u.src: My silken quilt cannot withstand the autumn wind; the waning water clock urges the autumn rain to greater haste.

p.src: Night after night it murmurs and sighs, as though beside the lamp it wept with one parted from her dear.

u.src: Night after night it murmurs and sighs, as though beside the lamp it wept with one parted from her dear.

p.src: Cold mist makes the little courtyard ever more forlorn; by sparse bamboo and an empty window, drops fall fitfully.

p.src: Who knows when the wind and rain will cease? Already my falling tears have soaked the window gauze.

p.src: When she had finished reciting, she laid down her brush and was just about to retire when a maid announced, “Master Bao has come.” Before she had finished speaking, Baoyu appeared, wearing a broad bamboo-leaf hat and a straw rain cape. Daiyu could not help laughing. “Where has this fisherman come from?” Baoyu hastily asked, “Are you feeling any better today? Have you taken your medicine? How much have you eaten all day?” As he spoke, he removed his hat and rain cape. Taking up the lamp in one hand and shielding its light with the other, he shone it upon Daiyu’s face, narrowed his eyes, and examined her closely. Then he smiled and said, “Your complexion looks a little better today.”

u.src: When she had finished reciting, she laid down her brush and was just about to retire when a maid announced, “Master Bao has come.”
Before she had finished speaking, Baoyu appeared, wearing a broad bamboo-leaf hat and a straw rain cape.
Daiyu could not help laughing. “Where has this fisherman come from?”
Baoyu hastily asked, “Are you feeling any better today?
Have you taken your medicine?
How much have you eaten all day?”

As he spoke, he removed his hat and rain cape. Taking up the lamp in one hand and shielding its light with the other, he shone it upon Daiyu’s face, narrowed his eyes, and examined her closely. Then he smiled and said, “Your complexion looks a little better today.”

p.src: After he had taken off his rain cape, Daiyu saw that beneath it he wore only a somewhat old short jacket of red damask, tied with a green sash. Below the knees showed dark-green silk trousers sprinkled with floral patterns; beneath them were padded gauze socks richly embroidered in gold, and on his feet he wore slippers patterned with butterflies and falling blossoms. Daiyu asked, “You are afraid of the rain above, but are those shoes and socks below not afraid of it? They are remarkably clean.” Baoyu laughed. “My rain gear is a complete set. There is also a pair of crabapple-wood clogs. I wore them here just now and left them beneath the veranda eaves.” Daiyu looked again and saw that the rain cape and hat were not ordinary articles sold in the marketplace, but exceedingly delicate and light. So she asked, “What kind of grass are they woven from? No wonder you do not look like a porcupine in them.” “All three pieces were gifts from the Prince of Beijing,” Baoyu replied. When he is at leisure at home on rainy days, he dresses like this too. If you like them, I will get another set and give it to you. The other pieces are nothing special, but this hat is amusing, for it actually comes apart. The crown at the top is detachable. In winter, when it snows, you wear a cap underneath, pull out the bamboo peg, and remove the crown, leaving only this brim. Both men and women can wear it in the snow. I will give you one to wear when it snows this winter.” Daiyu laughed. “I do not want one. If I wore that, I should look like a fisherwoman in a painting or on the stage.” Only after the words were out did she realize that she had spoken without reflection and that her remark paired her with the fisherman she had just called Baoyu. It was too late for regret. Her face flushed scarlet with embarrassment, and she bent over the table in an unceasing fit of coughing.

p.src: Baoyu, however, paid no heed to this. Catching sight of a poem on the table, he picked it up and read it through, then could not help exclaiming how good it was. Hearing him, Daiyu hurriedly rose, snatched it from his hand, and burned it in the lamp flame. Baoyu laughed. “I have already learned it by heart, so burning it will do no harm.” Daiyu said, “I am much better now too. Thank you for coming to see me several times a day, even when it is raining. It is late now, and I want to rest. You had better go home and come again tomorrow.” At this, Baoyu reached into his gown and took out a gold watch about the size of a walnut. He glanced at it and saw that the hand pointed to the time between the end of the Dog hour and the beginning of the Boar hour. He hastily tucked it away again and said, “It is indeed time you rested. I have kept you exerting yourself for half the day.” With that, he put on his rain cape and hat and went out, only to turn back and ask, “If there is anything you would like to eat, tell me. I can speak to the Old Lady first thing tomorrow morning. Would that not be clearer than leaving it to the old women?” Daiyu laughed. “If I think of anything tonight, I will tell you tomorrow morning. Listen, the rain is coming down harder. Hurry and go. Is there anyone accompanying you?” Two old women answered, “Yes. They are outside with umbrellas and a lit lantern.” Daiyu laughed. “A lantern in weather like this?” “It does not matter,” said Baoyu. “It is made of translucent horn and is not afraid of the rain.” Hearing this, Daiyu reached back and took a glass globe lantern from the bookshelf. She had a small candle lit inside it, then handed it to Baoyu, saying, “This one is brighter than that one and is made precisely for carrying in the rain.” Baoyu said, “I have one like this too, but I was afraid they might slip and fall and break it, so I did not have it lit and brought along.” Daiyu said, “Which matters more, breaking a lantern or hurting a person? Besides, you are not accustomed to wearing wooden clogs. Have them carry that lantern ahead to light the way. This one is light as well as bright and is meant to be carried personally in the rain. Would it not be better for you to carry it yourself? Bring it back tomorrow. Even if you drop it, the loss will be slight. Why have you suddenly developed this habit of cutting open your belly to save a pearl?” At this, Baoyu promptly took the lantern. Ahead of him went two old women carrying umbrellas and a translucent-horn lantern, while behind him came two young maids with umbrellas. Baoyu handed the lantern to one of the young maids to carry, steadied himself with a hand on her shoulder, and went straight away.

u.src: Baoyu, however, paid no heed to this. Catching sight of a poem on the table, he picked it up and read it through, then could not help exclaiming how good it was.
Hearing him, Daiyu hurriedly rose, snatched it from his hand, and burned it in the lamp flame.
Baoyu laughed. “I have already learned it by heart, so burning it will do no harm.”
Daiyu said, “I am much better now too. Thank you for coming to see me several times a day, even when it is raining.
It is late now, and I want to rest. You had better go home and come again tomorrow.”

At this, Baoyu reached into his gown and took out a gold watch about the size of a walnut. He glanced at it and saw that the hand pointed to the time between the end of the Dog hour and the beginning of the Boar hour. He hastily tucked it away again and said, “It is indeed time you rested. I have kept you exerting yourself for half the day.”

With that, he put on his rain cape and hat and went out, only to turn back and ask, “If there is anything you would like to eat, tell me. I can speak to the Old Lady first thing tomorrow morning. Would that not be clearer than leaving it to the old women?”
Daiyu laughed. “If I think of anything tonight, I will tell you tomorrow morning.
Listen, the rain is coming down harder. Hurry and go.
Is there anyone accompanying you?”
Two old women answered, “Yes. They are outside with umbrellas and a lit lantern.”
Daiyu laughed. “A lantern in weather like this?”
“It does not matter,” said Baoyu. “It is made of translucent horn and is not afraid of the rain.”

Hearing this, Daiyu reached back and took a glass globe lantern from the bookshelf. She had a small candle lit inside it, then handed it to Baoyu, saying, “This one is brighter than that one and is made precisely for carrying in the rain.”
Baoyu said, “I have one like this too, but I was afraid they might slip and fall and break it, so I did not have it lit and brought along.”
Daiyu said, “Which matters more, breaking a lantern or hurting a person?
Besides, you are not accustomed to wearing wooden clogs.
Have them carry that lantern ahead to light the way.
This one is light as well as bright and is meant to be carried personally in the rain. Would it not be better for you to carry it yourself?
Bring it back tomorrow.
Even if you drop it, the loss will be slight. Why have you suddenly developed this habit of cutting open your belly to save a pearl?”
At this, Baoyu promptly took the lantern. Ahead of him went two old women carrying umbrellas and a translucent-horn lantern, while behind him came two young maids with umbrellas.
Baoyu handed the lantern to one of the young maids to carry, steadied himself with a hand on her shoulder, and went straight away.

p.src: Just then, an old woman from All-spice Court arrived under an umbrella, carrying a lantern. She brought a large packet of the finest bird’s nest and another packet of fine powdered sugar, preserved plum slices, and snow-white foreign sugar. She said, “These are better than anything one can buy. Our young mistress said that you should eat these first, and she will send more when they are gone.” Daiyu said, “Go back and tell her I am most grateful for her thoughtfulness.” She told the servants to seat the woman outside and give her tea. The old woman laughed. “I will not stay for tea; I still have business to attend to.” Daiyu laughed. “I know how busy all of you are. Now that the weather is cool and the nights are long, all the more reason to gather for an all-night game and gamble to your hearts’ content for a few rounds.” The old woman laughed. “To tell you the truth, miss, I have been especially fortunate this year. In any case, several people must keep night watch in the different quarters each evening, and it would not do to miss calling the watches. We may as well gather for a night game: we keep watch at the same time and relieve our boredom too. Tonight I am the banker again. Now that the garden gates are shut, it is just about time to begin.” Hearing this, Daiyu laughed. “How good of you. You have braved the rain to make this delivery, even though it has delayed you from winning your fortune.” She ordered someone to give the woman a few hundred cash to buy some wine, so that she might ward off the chill and damp of the rain. The old woman laughed. “You are putting yourself to expense again, miss, by treating me to wine.” With that, she kowtowed once, received the money outside, and went away under her umbrella.

p.src: Zijuan put away the bird’s nest, then moved the lamp, lowered the curtains, and helped Daiyu settle down to sleep. Lying on her pillow, Daiyu reflected gratefully on Baochai. For a while she envied Baochai for having a mother and brother; then she thought that, although she and Baoyu had always been close, there would always be grounds for suspicion. Then she heard the rain pattering on the bamboo tips and withered leaves outside the window, while the clear chill seeped through the bed curtains; before she knew it, tears were falling once more. It was not until the fourth watch was nearly over that she gradually fell asleep. For the present, there is nothing more to tell. To learn what happened next, read the following chapter.
